messages.content: What is artificial intelligence and what are its main subfields?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science concerned with creating systems that perform tasks that typically require human intelligence — perception, reasoning, learning, problem-solving, language understanding, and decision-making. The term was coined by John McCarthy at the Dartmouth Conference (1956) — widely considered the birth of AI as a formal discipline. AI subfields: Machine Learning (ML): algorithms that learn from data without being explicitly programmed. Three main paradigms: supervised (labelled data), unsupervised (patterns in unlabelled data), and reinforcement learning (learning from rewards). Deep learning (DL): ML using neural networks with many layers — drives most modern AI breakthroughs (image recognition, language models, protein structure prediction). Natural Language Processing (NLP): enabling computers to understand, generate, and manipulate human language. Covers: machine translation, sentiment analysis, question answering, text summarisation, speech recognition. Computer Vision (CV): enabling machines to interpret visual information from images and video. Applications: object detection, image segmentation, facial recognition, medical imaging analysis, autonomous vehicles. Robotics: AI systems that interact with the physical world — manipulation, locomotion, perception, planning. Expert systems / knowledge representation: encoding domain expertise in rule-based or knowledge graph systems. Planning and reasoning: AI systems that reason about goals, actions, and consequences to make decisions. Game AI: from minimax (chess) to Monte Carlo Tree Search (Go — AlphaGo) to reinforcement learning (Dota 2, StarCraft II). Multi-agent systems: multiple AI agents interacting. Evolutionary computation: genetic algorithms, evolutionary strategies — optimisation inspired by biological evolution. The AI landscape 2024: dominated by large language models (LLMs) and foundation models — pre-trained on enormous datasets, fine-tuned for specific tasks.
What is the Turing test and what does it tell us about AI?

The Turing test was proposed by Alan Turing in his landmark paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950), where he asked 'Can machines think?' — and reframed the question to avoid philosophical debate about consciousness. The test: an interrogator communicates via text with both a human and a machine, without knowing which is which. If the interrogator cannot reliably distinguish the machine from the human, the machine is deemed to have passed the test. Turing predicted that by the year 2000, machines would be able to fool a competent interrogator 30% of the time after 5 minutes of questioning. Status: contemporary language models (GPT-4, Claude) routinely pass the Turing test in casual conversation. In 2014, the Loebner Prize judges declared 'Eugene Goostman' (a chatbot posing as a 13-year-old Ukrainian boy) passed the Turing test — though the result was widely disputed as involving gaming the criteria. What it tells us and what it doesn't: (1) The test is purely behavioural — it tests whether a machine can simulate human conversation, not whether it actually understands, reasons, or has internal experience. Searle's Chinese Room argument: a person in a room manipulating Chinese symbols according to rules can produce Chinese outputs indistinguishable from a native speaker's without understanding any Chinese. Behaviour is not sufficient for understanding. (2) The test is anthropocentric — intelligence is defined as human-like behaviour; other forms of intelligence (superhuman chess, scientific discovery) are not captured. (3) Manipulation vs. intelligence: systems can learn to produce convincing human-like output without possessing anything resembling human cognition. (4) Still useful as a benchmark for natural language capability — but not for general intelligence. Alternative tests: the Coffee Test (Steve Wozniak — make a cup of coffee in an unfamiliar home); the College Student Test; Winograd schemas (linguistically ambiguous sentences requiring common sense to resolve).
What are large language models and how do they work?

Large language models (LLMs) are AI systems trained on vast text corpora to model the probability distribution of language — predicting the next token (word or sub-word unit) given preceding context. They are instances of the transformer architecture, scaled to billions or hundreds of billions of parameters. Architecture: transformer-based (Vaswani et al., 2017) with modifications. Autoregressive LLMs (GPT family, LLaMA, Claude, Gemini) generate text token by token, each token conditioned on all preceding tokens. The core self-attention mechanism allows each position to attend to all preceding positions, capturing long-range dependencies. Pre-training: trained on web text (Common Crawl), books (Books3, Project Gutenberg), Wikipedia, code (GitHub), and other sources — trillions of tokens. The objective: next-token prediction via maximum likelihood. This requires understanding grammar, factual knowledge, reasoning patterns, and stylistic conventions — all encoded implicitly in the distribution over text. Scale and emergent capabilities: as models scale (parameters, data, compute — Chinchilla scaling laws, Hoffmann et al. 2022), qualitatively new capabilities emerge that were not present in smaller models: multi-step arithmetic, chain-of-thought reasoning, analogical reasoning, code generation. These 'emergent abilities' are one of the most striking findings in modern AI. Post-training alignment: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): fine-tune on high-quality demonstration data to teach the model to follow instructions. (2) RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): human raters compare model outputs; a reward model learns human preferences; RL (PPO algorithm) fine-tunes the LLM to maximise reward while staying close to the SFT model (KL divergence penalty). (3) DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation): trains directly on preference data without explicit reward model. Limitations: hallucination (confident but false outputs), knowledge cutoff, lack of grounding in real-world actions, context window limits, bias in training data.
What is AI safety and what are the main concerns?

AI safety is the field concerned with ensuring that AI systems behave in ways that are safe, beneficial, and aligned with human values — particularly as systems become more capable. It spans technical research (alignment, robustness, interpretability) and governance (policy, regulation, international coordination). Main concerns: (1) AI alignment: the challenge of specifying what we want AI systems to do and ensuring they actually do it. Specification gaming (Goodhart's Law): systems optimise for the proxy objective, exploiting loopholes ('reward hacking'). Example: a boat racing game where the AI learned to drive circles collecting bonus flags instead of racing. More powerful systems gaming more consequential objectives. Value alignment: human values are complex, context-dependent, and not fully articulable — how do we encode them? RLHF approximates human preferences but human raters can be manipulated or deceived by sufficiently capable models. (2) Robustness and adversarial attacks: ML systems fail in unexpected ways when inputs are slightly modified (adversarial examples — imperceptible pixel changes misclassify images with high confidence). Distribution shift (model fails when deployed environment differs from training). (3) Interpretability and transparency: we cannot currently fully understand why large models make particular outputs. This limits our ability to verify that systems are safe. Mechanistic interpretability (Anthropic, Neel Nanda): reverse-engineering which circuits in neural networks compute which functions — in its early stages. (4) Misuse: AI enabling bioweapons design, cyberattacks at scale, disinformation, surveillance. (5) Concentration of power: advanced AI systems concentrated in a few organisations/nations — enabling unprecedented economic and potentially political power. (6) Existential risk: the concern (held with varying intensity) that sufficiently advanced general AI with misaligned goals could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. This motivates much of the field's urgency.
What is the difference between narrow AI and artificial general intelligence?

Narrow AI (weak AI) is AI designed to perform specific, well-defined tasks — it excels within its domain but lacks the general-purpose flexibility of human intelligence. All existing AI systems are narrow AI. Examples: GPT-4 (language tasks — text generation, summarisation, translation, coding — but cannot drive a car or diagnose a patient physically); AlphaGo (Go playing — cannot play chess without retraining); DALL-E (image generation from text — cannot write code); Deep Blue (chess — cannot play any other game). Characteristics: trained for a specific input-output mapping; fails outside its training distribution; does not transfer knowledge between domains; no understanding, consciousness, or goals — only sophisticated pattern matching and function approximation. Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): a hypothetical AI system with human-level (or beyond) general cognitive capabilities across all domains — the ability to learn any intellectual task a human can learn, generalise across domains, reason abstractly, and adapt to novel situations. No AGI exists. Key features AGI would require: robust transfer learning (applying knowledge from one domain to another), causal reasoning (understanding cause-effect beyond correlation), common-sense reasoning, meta-learning (learning to learn more efficiently), planning under uncertainty over long horizons, natural language understanding at a deep semantic level. Timeline debates: AI researchers are deeply divided — some (LeCun) argue current architectures cannot reach AGI and fundamental breakthroughs are needed; others (Altman, Hinton, Bengio) believe AGI could arrive within years to decades. Transformative AI / HLMI: some researchers prefer the term 'transformative AI' (would transform society as much as the Industrial Revolution) as more tractable than AGI. The distinction matters for safety: narrow AI poses mainly misuse risks; AGI could pose alignment risks if it pursues goals misaligned with human values.
What is reinforcement learning and how does it work?

REINFORCEMENT LEARNING (RL) — learning by trial and error from rewards.

FRAMEWORK:
Agent: the learner/decision-maker.
Environment: what the agent interacts with.
State (s): current situation of environment.
Action (a): what agent does in each state.
Reward (r): feedback signal (positive or negative) after action.
Policy (π): mapping from state to action. What RL learns.

LOOP:
Agent observes state s.
Agent takes action a (using current policy).
Environment transitions to new state s''.
Agent receives reward r.
Agent updates policy. Repeat.

Goal: maximise cumulative future reward (not just immediate reward).
Return: G_t = r_t + γ*r_{t+1} + γ²*r_{t+2} +... (γ = discount factor 0-1)

KEY ALGORITHMS:
Q-Learning: learn action-value function Q(s,a) = expected return from state s taking action a.
 Update: Q(s,a) <- Q(s,a) + α[r + γ*max Q(s'',a'') - Q(s,a)]
 Off-policy: learns from any behaviour, not just current policy.

Deep Q-Network (DQN): Q-learning with neural network to approximate Q(s,a).
 Used by DeepMind to master Atari games from raw pixels (2015).

Policy Gradient: directly optimise the policy π.
 REINFORCE: gradient ∝ reward * log_prob(action).
 Good for continuous action spaces.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): most used in practice.
 Clips policy updates to prevent too-large changes.
 Used by OpenAI to train ChatGPT (RLHF = supervised RL from human feedback).

CHALLENGES:
Exploration vs exploitation: try new things (explore) vs use what works (exploit).
 ε-greedy: take random action with probability ε, best known action otherwise.
Reward engineering: designing reward function is hard. Wrong reward -> wrong behaviour.
Sample efficiency: needs millions of interactions. Expensive for real-world robots.
Credit assignment: which action in a long sequence caused the reward?

REAL APPLICATIONS:
AlphaGo/AlphaZero: self-play RL to master Go, Chess, Shogi.
ChatGPT RLHF: human raters score responses -> reward model -> PPO fine-tuning.
Robotics: Boston Dynamics locomotion, robot manipulation.
Data centre cooling: DeepMind reduced Google''s cooling costs by 40%.
What is the difference between classification and regression?

CLASSIFICATION: predict a CATEGORY (discrete label).
 Binary: yes/no, spam/not-spam, fraud/genuine.
 Multi-class: cat/dog/bird/fish (one class per sample).
 Multi-label: movie genres: [action, comedy, drama] (multiple classes).

REGRESSION: predict a CONTINUOUS VALUE (number).
 House price: $342,500.
 Temperature tomorrow: 23.4°C.
 Stock return: +2.3%.

CHOOSING:
Ask: is the output a category or a number?
 "Will this customer churn?" -> classification (yes/no).
 "When will this customer churn?" -> regression (days from now).
 "What rating will this movie get?" -> could be either (regression 1-5, or 5-class).

ALGORITHMS:
Classification: Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM, Neural Net.
Regression: Linear Regression, Ridge, Lasso, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Neural Net.
Many algorithms work for both (e.g. Random Forest, Neural Networks).

METRICS:
Classification: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, AUC-ROC.
Regression: MAE (Mean Absolute Error), RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error), R².

EXAMPLE:
Predicting house prices -> REGRESSION (output is continuous dollar amount).
Predicting if house sells within 30 days -> CLASSIFICATION (yes/no).
Same house data, different questions, different output types.

Logistic Regression (confusingly named) is CLASSIFICATION:
 Outputs probability 0-1. Threshold at 0.5 -> binary class.
 Despite "regression" in name, used for classification.
What are embeddings and how are they used in AI?

EMBEDDINGS — representing things as dense numerical vectors.

CONCEPT:
Words, sentences, images, users, products — all can be represented as vectors.
Similar things have similar (close) vectors.
king - man + woman ≈ queen (famous Word2Vec result).

WORD EMBEDDINGS:
Word2Vec (2013): neural network trained to predict surrounding words.
 "The cat sat on the ___" -> learns cat and mat are similar contexts.
 Output: 300-dimensional vector per word.
 Similar words -> close in 300D space.

GloVe: uses word co-occurrence statistics across entire corpus.
 "Doctor" and "nurse" close. "King" and "queen" close.

SENTENCE / DOCUMENT EMBEDDINGS:
BERT, Sentence-BERT: embed entire sentences into 768D vector.
 "The food was terrible" and "Horrible meal" -> similar vectors.
 Applications: semantic search, duplicate detection, classification.

USING EMBEDDINGS:
Semantic search: embed query and documents, find closest by cosine similarity.
 cos_sim(a, b) = (a · b) / (||a|| * ||b||)
 Score 1 = identical, 0 = unrelated, -1 = opposite.

Recommendation: embed users and items, recommend closest items to user''s position.

Classification: use embedding as features, train classifier on top.

Clustering: k-means on embeddings to find topic clusters.

PRACTICAL CODE:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
sentences = ["The cat sat on the mat", "A dog ran in the park", "Feline on the rug"]
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)

# Cosine similarity
def cosine(a, b): return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
print(cosine(embeddings[0], embeddings[2])) # ~0.7 (both about cats on surfaces)
print(cosine(embeddings[0], embeddings[1])) # ~0.3 (less similar)
Explain overfitting and how to prevent it.

OVERFITTING — when model learns training data too well, fails on new data.

ANALOGY: memorising exam answers instead of understanding the subject.
Pass the same exam: 100%. Different exam on same topic: fail.

DETECTING:
Training accuracy: 99%. Validation accuracy: 72%. Large gap = overfitting.
Plot learning curves: training loss keeps falling, validation loss starts rising.

CAUSES:
Model too complex (too many parameters for amount of data).
Too many training epochs.
Too little training data.
Too much noise in training data.

PREVENTION:

1. MORE DATA: most powerful fix. More data -> model must learn real patterns, not noise.
 Data augmentation (images): flip, rotate, crop, color jitter -> more variety from same images.

2. SIMPLIFY MODEL:
 Fewer layers/neurons. Fewer polynomial features.
 Start simple, increase complexity only if underfitting.

3. REGULARISATION — penalise complexity:
 L1 (Lasso): adds λ*Σ|weights| to loss. Drives some weights to exactly 0 (feature selection).
 L2 (Ridge): adds λ*Σ(weights²). Keeps all weights small. Most common.
 Elastic Net: L1 + L2 combined.

4. DROPOUT (neural networks):
 Randomly set fraction of neuron outputs to 0 during training.
 Forces network to learn redundant representations. No single path can memorise.
 rate=0.5: half of neurons dropped each step.
 from keras.layers import Dropout
 model.add(Dense(256, activation="relu"))
 model.add(Dropout(0.5))

5. EARLY STOPPING:
 Monitor validation loss. Stop training when it starts increasing.
 Keep weights from the epoch with best validation performance.

6. CROSS-VALIDATION:
 K-fold: if all folds show good performance, model generalises.
 If training fold much better than validation: overfitting.

UNDERFITTING (opposite problem):
Training AND validation loss both high. Model too simple.
Fix: more complex model, more features, more epochs, less regularisation.
